solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Well, it's right to have round tits

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A cheerful approval of a curvy figure.
explanation.walkthrough: "Well" reads as a throat-clearing interjection, but it is the adjective meaning healthy.
explanation.definitionFit: Well in the sense of healthy is a plain synonym of robust, both describing sound physical condition.

clue.text: Tories due for reconstruction, having no appetite ultimately for what Boris has become?

indicators.note: something up for reconstruction is to be rebuilt, so the letters go back together in a new order
having no appetite ultimately means that final letter is missing from the fodder

parts.note: due with its last letter E removed
the last letter of appetite, the letter taken out of due

explanation.surface: A jibe that the Tories need rebuilding and have lost their taste for Boris Johnson.
explanation.walkthrough: After his fall Boris Johnson was out of the party's inner circle, hence an outsider.
explanation.definitionFit: Once ousted from office, Johnson stood outside the government he had led, the sense of outsider the clue means.

clue.text: Outing a dopey thing to do?

definitions.meaning: an outing is a short excursion
dopey here means drugged: what someone on LSD does is hallucinate

explanation.surface: Asking whether a day out is a silly idea.
explanation.walkthrough: "Dopey" suggests foolish, but here it means drug-fuelled: a trip is a hallucinogenic experience.
explanation.definitionFit: Trip covers both a day out and a drug experience, the second sense being what dope might lead to.

clue.text: It might highlight king allying with EU in plan

indicators.note: 'in plan' places the king and EU inside the word for plan

parts.note: K is king in chess notation

explanation.surface: A political scheme in which a king forms an alliance with the European Union.
explanation.walkthrough: Highlighter is a make-up product, so the definition is fair.
explanation.definitionFit: By function: make-up products, highlighter among them, are used to accentuate facial features.

clue.text: Soft soap: dull attempt to conserve energy

indicators.note: to conserve something is to keep it safe inside, so the attempt holds the energy

parts.note: E is the symbol for energy

explanation.surface: A half-hearted effort to save energy.
explanation.walkthrough: Soft soap is an idiom for smooth persuasive praise, not a cleaning product.
explanation.definitionFit: Soft soap is an idiom for smooth, insincere praise, which is exactly what flattery names.

clue.text: Skilful operation — no bloke's work!

parts.note: a manoeuvre is a skilful move
a bloke is a man; removed

explanation.surface: Praise for a deft piece of work that no man could have done.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s joins the bloke to the work: take MAN from MANOEUVRE and the work is what remains.
explanation.definitionFit: Oeuvre is borrowed from French, where it simply means work; in English it names an artist's body of work.

clue.text: About to get worked up before girl finally gives a ride

parts.note: to arouse is to work up

explanation.surface: A saucy line in true Private Eye style about getting excited before a girl obliges.
explanation.walkthrough: The innuendo of "ride" is the misdirection; the answer is a fairground roundabout.
explanation.definitionFit: By example: a carousel, or merry-go-round, is one kind of fairground ride.

clue.text: see 26dn.
Citizen Suella's opening with a one-sided call for self-government

explanation.surface: Suella Braverman launching a lopsided bid for independence.
explanation.walkthrough: UDI is best known from Rhodesia's 1965 break from Britain; unilateral is the one-sided part.
explanation.definitionFit: By nationality: a Saudi is one kind of citizen, a national of Saudi Arabia.

clue.text: (& 12ac.) "Private Eye corrupt — sue 'em!" snapped conservative-biased government institution

parts.note: the magazine speaking of itself says us

indicators.note: snapped means broke or cracked, so the letters of the quoted words are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, part of the letters to rearrange
taken as written, the rest of the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A magazine's defiant cry to sue a corrupt court, blurted out against a partisan body.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye is a British satirical magazine, here talking about itself as US. 'snapped' shuffles CORRUPT with SUEEM.
explanation.definitionFit: The highest American court has a conservative majority of justices, so the setter calls that branch of government biased.

clue.text: Before court? Hard

parts.note: CT is the abbreviation for court

explanation.surface: A smutty question about arousal before wooing.
explanation.walkthrough: "Court" looks like the wooing verb but is only the abbreviation CT.
explanation.definitionFit: Hard and erect are near-synonyms for rigid and upright, with the innuendo the surface invites.

clue.text: see 10ac.
Time with current bedtime companion?

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time
an eddy is a swirling current

explanation.surface: Asking who your present partner in bed is.
explanation.walkthrough: "Current" reads as present-day, but it is a flow of water.
explanation.definitionFit: By example: a teddy bear is the classic toy a child takes to bed.

clue.text: "Could have been Edward Heath," May chants pathetically

indicators.note: pathetically means feebly and badly, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Theresa May sings feebly about what her predecessor Edward Heath might have been.
explanation.walkthrough: Edward Heath, a British Conservative prime minister of the 1970s, was a keen sailor who won the Sydney to Hobart race; 'pathetically' rearranges MAY CHANTS.
explanation.definitionFit: Heath raced his yacht Morning Cloud at the highest level, so he is a famous example of an ocean sailor.

clue.text: Talkative about sex, I nap — very English!

indicators.note: about here means around and all over the place, so these letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone holding forth about sex and an afternoon nap, in a very English way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like 'on the subject of', but it is the instruction to rearrange the words after it, giving EXPANSI before the two abbreviations follow.
explanation.definitionFit: An expansive person is open and communicative, ready to chat at length.

clue.text: Filthy rich on overtime, but without a bean

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so the other letters go round the A
filthy means dirty and messed up, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Someone stinking rich from overtime pay still has no money at all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without a bean' reads as penniless, but 'bean' is the definition and 'without' means outside. 'Filthy' gives HRIC, and the letters go round the A.
explanation.definitionFit: The haricot is a type of French bean, the white seed used for baked beans.

clue.text: Rein in your expectations, being crap

definitions.meaning: read as an instruction to expect less
crap in the slang sense of useless

explanation.surface: Advice to expect less of something that is rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition is read as an instruction: hope less.
explanation.definitionFit: Crap as slang means useless, which is hopeless; the other half splits the word into hope less.

clue.text: One's covered in dynamic fat

indicators.note: one covered in something is wrapped by it

explanation.surface: Someone smeared in a lively sort of grease.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is "is": one is covered by PUNCHY.
explanation.definitionFit: Paunchy means having a pot belly, so it is a narrower synonym of fat.

clue.text: Take steps to overturn state cut-back

indicators.note: cut-back says the word for cut is read backwards

parts.note: to lop is to cut off

indicators.note: to overturn means to turn upside down, so in a down answer the letters are read upwards

parts.note: AK is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Alaska

explanation.surface: A call to action to reverse a government's spending cuts.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a verb: to dance this lively 19th-century step. 'cut-back' gives the reversed word for cut, and 'overturn' turns the state's abbreviation upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: To polka is to dance the polka, a lively Bohemian dance, so it is a way of stepping out.

clue.text: Windy thing moderates article about 'Johnson's end'

indicators.note: to moderate something is to alter it, so the article's letters are changed round
about means around, so the jumbled letters go round Johnson's end

explanation.surface: A long-winded type tones down a news piece on Boris Johnson's downfall.
explanation.walkthrough: "Windy thing" suggests a bore, but it is a wind instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: Wind instruments are played by breath, so a clarinet is one jokily called a windy thing.

clue.text: Partisan CIA contrived, with IT, to intervene in vote

indicators.note: something contrived is artfully put together, so the letters are arranged anew
to intervene is to come between, so the jumble goes inside the vote

explanation.surface: The CIA using technology to meddle in an election.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface describes election meddling, and the answer describes the surface: such interference is itself partisan.
explanation.definitionFit: Partisan means taking one side, and political bias is the commonest sense.

clue.text: Ready to stick top of cock in carrot?

indicators.note: to stick something in is to push it inside, so one piece goes within another
in says where the letter is stuck: inside the word for carrot

parts.note: a carrot is an inducement, a lure

indicators.note: the top of a word in a down clue is its first letter

explanation.surface: A smutty question about sticking something into a carrot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ready' is British slang for cash, as in 'ready money'; 'carrot' is the reward dangled before a donkey, a lure. 'top of' gives C, and 'to stick' it 'in' the lure.
explanation.definitionFit: Lucre is money, especially ill-gotten gain, and the ready means cash to hand.

clue.text: Conservative louse appropriates state formal wear?

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for Conservative

indicators.note: to appropriate is to take into one's own keeping

parts.note: a louse is a rotter, a rat

explanation.surface: A Tory scoundrel helping himself to state money for smart clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: "Louse" is a contemptible person here, not an insect; VA is the US abbreviation for Virginia.
explanation.definitionFit: By example: a cravat is a smart neckcloth, one item of formal wear.

clue.text: March will see change of heart by presidential candidate?

indicators.note: a change of heart means the middle letter is swapped for another

parts.note: Donald Trump, a US presidential candidate

explanation.surface: A political prediction that a candidate will alter his views in March.
explanation.walkthrough: 'March' looks like the month, but it is a verb meaning to hike; 'will see change of heart' swaps the middle U of TRUMP for A.
explanation.definitionFit: To tramp is to walk heavily or trudge a long way, which is to march.

clue.text: Number one covering up plonker's slight

indicators.note: covering something up hides it underneath

parts.note: number one is a childish word for a pee
a plonker and a tit are both fools

explanation.surface: A top person hushing up an idiot's minor insult.
explanation.walkthrough: "Number one" looks like the boss; plonker is British slang for an idiot.
explanation.definitionFit: Petite, borrowed from French for small, describes a slight, small-framed build.

clue.text: Deputy's dire column — finish off

indicators.note: something in a dire state is a mess, so the letters are jumbled
to finish off is to kill, so the column's finish, its last letter, goes

explanation.surface: A deputy writer's dreadful newspaper piece being killed off.
explanation.walkthrough: A locum is a stand-in doctor or cleric.
explanation.definitionFit: A locum, short for locum tenens, stands in for an absent doctor or cleric, so deputy is a synonym.

clue.text: Archer isn't a shit? — er, chucked out, he'd cause disorder

indicators.note: as slang for rubbish, a shit version of the letters is a mess of them
something chucked out is thrown away, so ER leaves ARCHER

explanation.surface: A hesitant defence of Jeffrey Archer, the Tory novelist jailed for perjury.
explanation.walkthrough: The "er" looks like a stammer but is the pair of letters to remove.
explanation.definitionFit: An anarchist opposes all government, and the definition describes him by what he would bring about.

clue.text: & 8dn.) House rules often ignored — "poorly concocted, found to lack precision, ultimately"

definitions.note: the cross-reference adds 8 down to this light, so the definition covers the whole phrase

indicators.note: poorly means badly made, so the letters are rearranged
to lack means to be without, so a letter is taken out of the pool before rearranging

parts.note: taken as written, part of the pool of letters
taken as written, the rest of the pool

indicators.note: ultimately points to the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A jibe at a set of parliamentary rules, badly drafted and vague, that members routinely flout.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: CONCOCTED plus FOUND, 'to lack' the N that 'ultimately' takes from 'precision', is what 'poorly' rearranges. It is a jab at Westminster's rules on MPs' behaviour.
explanation.definitionFit: A code of conduct is a set of rules for behaviour, which in a House of Parliament politicians often disregard.

clue.text: Grand in sweaty pants?

indicators.note: pants is British slang for rubbish, so these letters are a mess to rearrange

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A question about something large inside perspiring underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pants' looks like underwear (in British English pants are underpants), but here it is the slang for rubbish, signalling that IN SWEATY is to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A Steinway is a famous make of piano, and a grand is the full-size kind of piano.

clue.text: Reduced commercial trade in trouble — Vladimir's first to butt in

indicators.note: to butt in is to push in uninvited, so one letter goes inside the others
in trouble means in a mess, so the letters of the word are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the letters to rearrange

indicators.note: first means the opening letter of the name

explanation.surface: Trade sanctions bite as Putin pushes his way into the dispute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Vladimir' brings Putin to mind, but 'first' only takes his V, which 'to butt in' places inside ADERT, the letters of TRADE 'in trouble'.
explanation.definitionFit: Advert is the clipped, shortened form of advertisement, the commercial in full.
